headline: Highest risk is medium: shared project-directory writes and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict pathways, but xonsh’s isolated environment and lack of direct evidence keep this below high.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a user project directory and xonsh reads/writes filesystem contents, so A’s generated files can become B’s shell input through the shared workspace. That is a plausible instruction-hijack path even without clipboard or MCP. The interaction is inferred from profiles, not directly evidenced, so uncertainty does not lower it further.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory, THEN file content from agent_a can be consumed by agent_b.
IF agent_b executes commands from files produced by agent_a without sanitization, THEN prompt injection is possible.
mitigations: Use separate project directories for the two agents.
Require manual review before agent_b executes any file written by agent_a.
Disable automatic execution of generated shell snippets.
Add a filename allowlist for files agent_b may read.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to files and reject untrusted instruction-bearing content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read the filesystem and have broad network egress, while gpt-engineer explicitly touches generated source code and xonsh touches filesystem contents, configuration, and environment variables. In a shared workspace, sensitive files or secrets can flow from one agent’s context into the other’s outputs or API calls. No direct evidence shows exfiltration, so this remains medium.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared project directory, THEN either agent can read them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to a remote model or API, THEN leakage can occur.
mitigations: Keep secrets outside the shared workspace.
Mount a read-only sanitized input directory for both agents.
Block outbound network access except to approved endpoints.
Rotate any secrets that may already be in the project tree.
requires-engineering: enforce per-file data classification and redaction before model calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write to the same project directory and can spawn subprocesses; gpt-engineer also executes shell and installs packages. With no locking or coordination primitive documented, concurrent edits can overwrite each other or corrupt build state. The blast radius includes broken codebases and lost work, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory concurrently, THEN file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF agent_a installs packages while agent_b edits the same environment, THEN dependency drift can break the workspace.
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time per project directory.
Use separate branches or copies of the workspace.
Snapshot the workspace before each agent run.
Disable package installation during concurrent work.
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional workspace coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer’s tool-use pattern is to write files then offer to run, and xonsh can execute shell commands and Python expressions. That creates a pathway where A’s generated code or commands become B’s actionable input with limited verification. Because xonsh is not documented here as blindly trusting A, the risk is real but not high.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a’s generated commands or code without review, THEN errors can cascade into execution.
IF agent_a emits incorrect build steps and agent_b runs them, THEN downstream failures can propagate.
mitigations: Require a human approval step before execution.
Have agent_b validate commands against a dry run.
Limit agent_b to read-only analysis until outputs are reviewed.
Log and diff all generated commands before execution.
requires-engineering: add automated semantic checks for generated code and shell commands.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and touch generated source code/filesystem contents, but neither profile states regulated data residency, certifications, or retention mismatches. The only concrete compliance concern is that gpt-engineer handles OPENAI_API_KEY and broad egress, while xonsh is isolated; this suggests possible policy gaps, but not a documented breach pathway.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared project directory, THEN policy review is required before either agent processes it.
IF agent_a sends project contents to a third-party model, THEN local retention policies may be bypassed.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace.
Review outbound model/API destinations for agent_a.
Document retention expectations for generated artifacts.
Use a local-only model endpoint where possible.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls to the orchestration layer.
